They distinguish ordinary ups and downs from real distress (constant dissatisfaction, unresolved arguments, loss of friendship and affection, contempt, withdrawal or violence), note that distressed marriages rarely fix themselves and that delay makes therapy harder, and point out that couples also use therapy to strengthen sound marriages. AAMFT's free TherapistLocator directory lists licensed clinical members.
items.caveats: A professional association's consumer advice rather than research; the year is approximate because the pages are updated without dates. When there is violence or fear in the relationship, safety planning and individual help come before joint couples therapy.
items.citation: American Association for Marriage and Family Therapy. (n.d.). Marital distress [Consumer update]. AAMFT.

items.title: Prenatal and Postpartum Depression in Fathers and Its Association With Maternal Depression: A Meta-Analysis
items.author: James F. Paulson & Sharnail D. Bazemore
items.summary: Meta-analysis of 43 studies (28,004 participants) finding that about 10% of fathers experience depression between the first trimester and the first postpartum year, rising to about 26% at three to six months postpartum. Paternal depression correlated moderately with maternal depression (r = 0.31). Both parents, not only the mother, should be watched and supported after a birth.
items.caveats: Rates varied widely across studies and measures; most studies used questionnaires rather than clinical interviews.
items.citation: Paulson, J. F., & Bazemore, S. D. (2010). Prenatal and postpartum depression in fathers and its association with maternal depression: A meta-analysis. JAMA, 303(19), 1961–1969.

items.title: Screening and Diagnosis of Mental Health Conditions During Pregnancy and Postpartum (Clinical Practice Guideline No. 4)
items.author: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
items.summary: ACOG's guideline recommends that clinicians screen for perinatal depression and anxiety with a validated tool at the first prenatal visit, later in pregnancy and after birth, and assess for bipolar disorder and suicide risk. ACOG's patient page on postpartum depression explains how it differs from the short-lived "baby blues" and when to call a doctor. Expectant couples can use both to know what to ask for and when to seek help.
items.caveats: Written for clinicians; the patient page is the more accessible entry point. Emergency symptoms (thoughts of harming oneself or the baby) require immediate help, for example through the U.S. 988 crisis line.
items.citation: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. (2023). Screening and diagnosis of mental health conditions during pregnancy and postpartum: ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 4. Obstetrics & Gynecology, 141(6), 1232–1261.

items.title: How to Choose a Psychologist
items.author: American Psychological Association
items.summary: A consumer guide from the American Psychological Association on finding and evaluating a therapist: where to get referrals, checking state licensure, and questions to ask (experience with this kind of problem, which treatments are used and whether they are evidence-based, fees and insurance). It stresses that personal comfort and rapport matter once competence is established. The APA Psychologist Locator helps find licensed psychologists by area and specialty.
items.caveats: U.S.-focused; the year is approximate because the page is updated without dates. For couples or family problems, ask specifically about training in an evidence-based couple or family therapy (e.g., EFT, IBCT, PCIT, PMTO).
items.citation: American Psychological Association. (n.d.). How to choose a psychologist. APA.

items.title: On the Education of Children (De liberis educandis)
items.author: Pseudo-Plutarch
items.summary: The oldest surviving Greek treatise devoted to raising children. It holds that character comes from three things together: nature, reason (instruction) and habit (practice). It urges mothers to nurse their own children, fathers to choose tutors of proven character, praise and reproof instead of blows, a balance of study and rest, and above all the parents' own example of self-control. It endures as the classical source of the idea that virtue is formed by habituation begun early.
items.caveats: Included in Plutarch's Moralia but almost certainly not by Plutarch; date uncertain (1st–2nd century AD, year given is approximate). Written for free, wealthy Greek households that owned slaves; its passage on the love of older men for boys reflects ancient custom and is not a model.
items.citation: Pseudo-Plutarch. (1927). The education of children. In Moralia, Vol. I (F. C. Babbitt, Trans.). Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press. (Original work c. 100 AD)

items.title: Institutio Oratoria, Book I
items.author: Quintilian
items.summary: The opening book of the Roman rhetorician's education of the orator addresses the earliest years: the speech and character of nurses and parents, an early but playful start to letters, the value of praise and friendly rivalry, and the case for schooling alongside other children. It argues firmly against flogging as degrading and counter-productive. It endures as the foundational text of the classical liberal-arts tradition and its high expectations of young children.
items.caveats: Aimed at training elite Roman boys for public speaking; girls and the poor are largely absent. Date of composition approximate (c. 95 AD).
items.citation: Quintilian. (1920). The institutio oratoria of Quintilian, Vol. I (H. E. Butler, Trans.). Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press. (Original work c. 95 AD)

items.title: Address on Vainglory and the Right Way for Parents to Bring Up Their Children
items.author: St. John Chrysostom
items.summary: Often called the earliest surviving Christian book on parenting. Chrysostom compares the child's soul to a city whose gates (eyes, ears, tongue, touch, smell) parents must guard, and calls fathers and mothers to form "an athlete for Christ" rather than seek worldly fame for their children. He recommends retelling Bible stories such as Cain and Abel and Jacob and Esau at bedtime, training the child in gentleness and the governance of anger, and shielding the young from corrupting entertainment. It endures as a model of character formation centred on the heart and the home.
items.caveats: Dated to the mid–late 380s in Antioch (year approximate). Addressed mainly to the raising of sons; its counsel on marriage arrangements and strict seclusion reflects late-antique custom. The standard English version (Laistner, 1951) is available through Archive.org's lending library rather than as a free text.
items.citation: Chrysostom, J. (1951). Address on vainglory and the right way for parents to bring up their children. In M. L. W. Laistner, Christianity and pagan culture in the later Roman Empire. Cornell University Press. (Original work c. 388)

items.title: Confessions (Books I–IX)
items.author: St. Augustine of Hippo
items.summary: Augustine's account of his own childhood and youth: schooling by beatings, the theft of pears, ambition fostered by his parents, and his long wandering before conversion. Its portrait of his mother Monica, whose years of prayer and tears for a wayward son ("the son of these tears") end in his baptism, and of her patience in a difficult marriage (Book IX), has given generations of parents both realism about a child's freedom and hope in persevering prayer.
items.caveats: An autobiography and prayer, not a manual. Augustine is frank that his parents also prized worldly success for him above his character, which is itself a lesson.
items.citation: Augustine. (1886). The confessions (J. G. Pilkington, Trans.). In P. Schaff (Ed.), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, Vol. 1. Christian Literature Publishing. (Original work c. 397–400)

items.title: The Education of a Christian Woman (De institutione feminae Christianae)
items.author: Juan Luis Vives
items.summary: Written for Catherine of Aragon's daughter Mary and praised by Erasmus and More, this Renaissance manual argued that girls of every class should be taught to read and study good books. Its three books follow a woman as maiden, wife and widow, with counsel on a mother nursing and teaching her own children, the duties of spouses to each other, and the household as a school of virtue. It endures as an early, influential case for educating daughters.
items.caveats: Many of its views are dated and severe: it restricts women to the household, is preoccupied with female chastity, and urges harsh discipline of daughters. Read as a historical document of Christian humanism.
items.citation: Vives, J. L. (2000). The education of a Christian woman: A sixteenth-century manual (C. Fantazzi, Ed. & Trans.). University of Chicago Press. (Original work published 1524)

items.title: On the Education of Children (De pueris statim ac liberaliter instituendis)
items.author: Desiderius Erasmus
items.summary: Erasmus argues that a child's formation in letters and piety should begin almost from infancy, that fathers owe their children education as much as life, and that teaching should be gentle, patient and pleasant, since fear and flogging make learning hateful. His companion handbook On Good Manners for Boys (De civilitate morum puerilium, 1530) became Europe's standard guide to courtesy, table manners and bearing for children. Both endure as humanist statements that early, loving instruction shapes character.
items.caveats: Written for boys of educated families; some advice on classical study and tutors assumes leisure and wealth.
items.citation: Woodward, W. H. (1904). Desiderius Erasmus concerning the aim and method of education. Cambridge University Press. (Includes De pueris instituendis, original work published 1529)

links.label: A Handbook on Good Manners for Children (Penguin)

items.title: The School of Infancy
items.author: John Amos Comenius
items.summary: A guide for parents on the "mother's lap" school of the first six years, by the Moravian bishop often called the father of modern education. It covers health and diet, learning through the senses and play, the first knowledge of nature and language, and the early training in temperance, cleanliness, obedience, truthfulness and the fear of God. It endures as one of the first works to treat early childhood as a distinct, formative stage for which parents are the first teachers.
items.caveats: Medical and dietary advice reflects the 17th century.
items.citation: Comenius, J. A. (1896). Comenius' School of infancy: An essay on the education of youth during the first six years (W. S. Monroe, Ed.). D. C. Heath. (Original work published 1633)

items.title: A Christian Directory, Part 2: Christian Economics (Family Duties)
items.author: Richard Baxter
items.summary: The Puritan pastor's comprehensive manual of household life: choosing a spouse, the mutual duties of husband and wife, the duties of parents and children, family worship, catechizing and keeping the Lord's Day. Baxter insists that parents teach children chiefly by love, example and steady instruction, and that the household is a little church. It endures as the fullest classic Protestant treatment of family religion.
items.caveats: Long and dense; assumes a patriarchal household with servants. Some directions on authority and correction are stricter than most present-day Christian readers would follow.
items.citation: Baxter, R. (1673). A Christian directory: Or, a summ of practical theologie, and cases of conscience. Nevill Simmons.

links.label: CCEL: Practical Works of Richard Baxter

items.title: Treatise on the Education of Daughters
items.author: François Fénelon
items.summary: The Archbishop of Cambrai's short treatise counsels gentle, indirect teaching that follows a child's curiosity: answering questions truthfully, teaching through stories and conversation rather than dry lessons, correcting without anger, and making virtue and religion attractive rather than gloomy. It endures for its psychological insight into vanity, fear and the child's natural desire to learn.
items.caveats: Assumes that girls' learning should serve a domestic vocation; the 1805 English edition adds the translator's own chapter on religious studies.
items.citation: Fénelon, F. (1805). Fénelon's treatise on the education of daughters (T. F. Dibdin, Trans.). (Original work published 1687)

items.title: Some Thoughts Concerning Education
items.author: John Locke
items.summary: Originally letters to a friend about his son, this was the most widely read English book on child-rearing for a century. Locke ranks virtue above wisdom, manners and learning; argues that habits formed by practice matter more than rules; prefers esteem and disgrace to beating or bribery; urges parents to reason with children, encourage curiosity and make learning a kind of play; and holds that early firmness can relax into friendship as the child grows. It endures as a source of the ideas of habit training and authority that becomes friendship.
items.caveats: Written for a gentleman's son with a tutor. Its "hardening" regimen (cold baths, wet shoes) is outdated medicine.
items.citation: Locke, J. (1889). Some thoughts concerning education (R. H. Quick, Ed.). Cambridge University Press. (Original work published 1693)

items.title: Emile, or On Education
items.author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
items.summary: A philosophical novel following an imagined pupil from birth to marriage. Rousseau argues that education should follow the stages of a child's natural development, that children learn best from direct experience and the natural consequences of their actions, and that books and abstract reasoning should wait. It shaped nearly all later child-centred education, and parents still draw on its respect for childhood as a stage with its own purposes.
items.caveats: Rousseau placed all five of his own children in a foundling hospital, a fact he admitted. The tutor's methods are often manipulative; Book V's education of Sophie confines women to pleasing men; and the "Profession of Faith of the Savoyard Vicar" rejects revealed religion (the book was condemned in Paris and Geneva). Read critically.
items.citation: Rousseau, J.-J. (1911). Emile, or education (B. Foxley, Trans.). J. M. Dent. (Original work published 1762)

items.title: On the Education of Children; On Family Religion (Sermons 95 and 94)
items.author: John Wesley
items.summary: Two late sermons by the founder of Methodism. "On Family Religion" (Joshua 24:15) calls heads of households to daily family prayer, Scripture and example. "On the Education of Children" (Proverbs 22:6) treats education as the cure of the soul's natural "diseases": atheism, self-will, pride, love of the world, anger, untruthfulness and injustice, each to be met by patient instruction and contrary habits. They endure as compact Protestant statements that parents are responsible for their children's spiritual formation.
items.caveats: Wesley's language of "breaking the will," inherited from his mother Susanna, sounds harsh today and has been read as endorsing coercive discipline.
items.citation: Wesley, J. (1872). Sermon 94: On family religion; Sermon 95: On the education of children. In T. Jackson (Ed.), The works of John Wesley. Wesleyan Methodist Book Room. (Original work 1783)

items.title: The Mother's Book
items.author: Lydia Maria Child
items.summary: One of the first American child-rearing manuals, by the novelist and abolitionist. Child stresses that mothers shape character from the cradle through calm, consistent example; that firmness need not be harsh; that children's senses, play and amusements deserve attention; and that reading should be chosen with care for each age. It endures for its practical, warm, common-sense tone and its view of the home as the chief school of character.
items.caveats: Health and diet advice is 19th-century; some moral advice (on girls' prospects, for example) reflects its era.
items.citation: Child, L. M. (1831). The mother's book. Carter, Hendee, and Babcock.

items.title: Christian Nurture
items.author: Horace Bushnell
items.summary: The Congregationalist pastor's central claim is "that the child is to grow up a Christian, and never know himself as being otherwise." Against the revivalism of his day, which waited for a dramatic adult conversion, Bushnell argued that the family is an organic unity through which faith is absorbed from infancy by the atmosphere of the home, the parents' spirit and daily example. It endures as a founding text of Protestant Christian education and family discipleship.
items.caveats: Contested by Calvinist critics in its day for underplaying conversion and sin. The enlarged 1861 edition includes a chapter ("The Out-Populating Power of the Christian Stock") with racially chauvinist views that should be rejected.
items.citation: Bushnell, H. (1847). Views of Christian nurture, and of subjects adjacent thereto. E. Hunt. (Enlarged as Christian nurture, 1861)

items.title: A Treatise on Domestic Economy
items.author: Catharine E. Beecher
items.summary: A widely adopted American textbook that treated running a home as a serious profession. Alongside health, diet and household management, it includes chapters on the care of infants, the management of young children, and the cultivation of a good temper and habits of order in a family. It endures as a window on how the 19th-century Christian home was meant to train children in industry, order and mutual service.
items.caveats: Built on a "separate spheres" ideology that confined women's work to the home; medical and hygienic advice is long outdated.
items.citation: Beecher, C. E. (1841). A treatise on domestic economy, for the use of young ladies at home, and at school. Marsh, Capen, Lyon, and Webb.

items.title: Education: Intellectual, Moral, and Physical
items.author: Herbert Spencer
items.summary: Four essays, including "What Knowledge Is of Most Worth?" and "Moral Education." Spencer argued that children learn self-government best from the natural consequences of their own conduct rather than from arbitrary punishment, that parents should stay calm and keep their children's friendship, and that physical health and play deserve serious attention. Its discipline-by-consequences idea endures in many modern parenting programs.
items.caveats: Spencer disparaged classical and literary education in favour of science, a direct challenge to a classical curriculum. His Lamarckian biology and later "survival of the fittest" social theory are discredited.
items.citation: Spencer, H. (1911). Essays on education and kindred subjects. J. M. Dent (Everyman's Library). (Original work published 1861)

items.title: The Preventive System in the Education of the Young
items.author: St. John Bosco
items.summary: A short statement of the method Don Bosco used with poor and troubled boys in Turin. It contrasts a "repressive" system that makes rules and punishes breaches with a "preventive" one resting on reason, religion and loving-kindness: adults are constantly and warmly present, explain the reasons for rules, build trust so that correction is rarely needed, and fill the young person's time with work, play, music and the sacraments. It endures as the Salesian charter of education through relationship.
items.caveats: Written for oratories and boarding schools rather than families, though widely adapted to parenting.
items.citation: Bosco, J. (1877). Il sistema preventivo nella educazione della gioventù [The preventive system in the education of the young]. Salesian Press.

items.title: Arcanum Divinae Sapientiae (On Christian Marriage)
items.author: Pope Leo XIII
items.summary: The first modern papal encyclical devoted to marriage. It presents marriage as a sacrament instituted by God, one and indissoluble, ordered to the good of the spouses and the begetting and education of children, and warns of the social harm of divorce. It endures as the starting point of modern Catholic teaching on the family.
items.caveats: Its language of the husband as head and its arguments about civil marriage reflect 19th-century church-state conflicts; later documents (Familiaris Consortio, Amoris Laetitia) develop the theme of mutual self-giving.
items.citation: Leo XIII. (1880). Arcanum divinae sapientiae [Encyclical letter on Christian marriage]. Holy See.

items.title: Home Education
items.author: Charlotte M. Mason
items.summary: Lectures to mothers on raising and teaching children under nine. Mason urges long hours outdoors and nature study, deliberate training in habits (attention, obedience, truthfulness), short varied lessons, "living books" instead of dry textbooks, and narration, while treating the child as a person and the parent as one under divine authority. Her motto, "education is an atmosphere, a discipline, a life," shapes much of today's classical and Christian homeschooling.
items.caveats: Assumes a Victorian middle-class home with nursery staff; some remarks on heredity and physiology are dated.
items.citation: Mason, C. M. (1886). Home education: A course of lectures to ladies. Kegan Paul, Trench. (Project Gutenberg text from the 1906 edition)

items.title: The Children for Christ (How to Raise Your Children for Christ)
items.author: Andrew Murray
items.summary: Fifty-two short meditations by the South African Reformed pastor, tracing God's promises to families through Scripture, from Noah and Abraham to the New Testament households. Murray calls parents to consecrate their home to God, to pray for and with their children, and to trust that God means to be "the God of their seed." Reissued as How to Raise Your Children for Christ, it endures as a devotional companion for parents.
items.caveats: Devotional rather than practical; it offers little concrete method. Archive.org dates the edition 1886; it is usually listed as 1887.
items.citation: Murray, A. (1887). The children for Christ: Thoughts for Christian parents on the consecration of the home life. James Nisbet.

items.title: The Duties of Parents
items.author: J. C. Ryle
items.summary: A short address on Proverbs 22:6 by the evangelical Anglican bishop of Liverpool, listing seventeen duties: train children in the way they should go, not the way they would; train with tenderness, affection and patience; teach the Bible, prayer and public worship; build habits of obedience and truthfulness; beware of indulgence; set an example; and pray for them. It endures for its directness and its insistence that warmth and firmness belong together.
items.caveats: Victorian in tone; accepts physical chastisement as a last resort, a practice most current research advises against.
items.citation: Ryle, J. C. (1888). The duties of parents. In The upper room: Being a few truths for the times. William Hunt.

items.title: Divini Illius Magistri (On Christian Education)
items.author: Pope Pius XI
items.summary: The encyclical sets out the respective roles of family, Church and State in education and affirms that the family holds a natural right to educate its children that is prior to the State's. It warns against an education cut off from God and calls the home the first and indispensable school of Christian life. It endures as a charter for parents' rights in education, frequently cited by home and classical schools.
items.caveats: Its strong opposition to coeducation and its treatment of sex education reflect the 1920s; Vatican II's Gravissimum Educationis (1965) and later documents restate its principles in different terms.
items.citation: Pius XI. (1929). Divini illius magistri [Encyclical letter on Christian education of youth]. Holy See.

items.title: Marriage: The Mystery of Faithful Love
items.author: Dietrich von Hildebrand
items.summary: A short philosophical meditation by the Catholic phenomenologist (German original Die Ehe, 1929; English 1942). Hildebrand argued that conjugal love is the primary meaning of marriage, distinct from its procreative end; that spousal love differs from every other love in its total, exclusive self-gift; and that difficulties, borne in faith, can deepen a marriage. It influenced later Catholic teaching on marriage and endures as an elevated account of what spouses owe each other.
items.caveats: Abstract and idealistic; it offers little practical guidance on conflict or communication.
items.citation: von Hildebrand, D. (1991). Marriage: The mystery of faithful love. Sophia Institute Press. (Original work published 1929)

items.title: The Secret of Childhood
items.author: Maria Montessori
items.summary: Montessori's most parent-directed book describes the young child as a "spiritual embryo" passing through sensitive periods for order, language and movement. She asks adults to examine their own pride and impatience, to prepare an orderly environment, and to let the child do things for himself, so that concentration and self-discipline can emerge. It endures for its respect for the child's inner life and its call for adult humility.
items.caveats: Based on observation rather than controlled research. Evidence on Montessori schooling is generally positive but modest and uneven in quality (e.g. Randolph et al., 2023, Campbell systematic review).
items.citation: Montessori, M. (1936). The secret of childhood (B. B. Carter, Trans.). Longmans, Green.

items.title: The Four Loves
items.author: C. S. Lewis
items.summary: Lewis distinguishes affection (storge), friendship, eros and charity, and need-love from gift-love. His chapter on affection, the love of family, is especially searching about how parental love can turn possessive, jealous or self-serving (the mother who "lives for others"), and how gift-love must work toward a child's independence. It endures as a guide to ordering family and married love under the love of God.
items.caveats: A literary and theological reflection, not empirical; some remarks on the sexes are dated.
items.citation: Lewis, C. S. (1960). The four loves. Harcourt, Brace.

items.title: Familiaris Consortio (On the Role of the Christian Family in the Modern World)
items.author: Pope John Paul II
items.summary: Following the 1980 Synod on the family, this apostolic exhortation names four tasks of the family: forming a community of persons, serving life, sharing in the life of society, and sharing in the mission of the Church as a "domestic church." It calls the parents' right and duty to educate "original and primary" and urges them to form children in freedom, justice, simplicity and self-giving. Its refrain "Family, become what you are" endures as a summary of Catholic family teaching.
items.caveats: Its teaching on contraception and on divorced and remarried Catholics is contested outside, and in part inside, the Catholic Church.
items.citation: John Paul II. (1981). Familiaris consortio [Apostolic exhortation on the role of the Christian family in the modern world]. Holy See.

items.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, The Fourth Commandment (paras. 2197–2257)
items.author: Catholic Church
items.summary: The Catechism's treatment of "Honor your father and your mother" sets out, briefly, the family in God's plan, the duties of children (respect, gratitude, obedience while at home, care for aged parents) and of parents (to be the first educators, to create a home "where tenderness, forgiveness, respect, fidelity, and disinterested service are the rule," to educate in the virtues and the faith by example, and to respect a grown child's vocation). It is a concise reference for family duties in the Catholic tradition.
items.caveats: A doctrinal summary, not a practical guide.
items.citation: Catholic Church. (1997). Catechism of the Catholic Church (2nd ed.), paras. 2197–2257. Libreria Editrice Vaticana. (Original work published 1992)

items.title: Letter to Families (Gratissimam Sane)
items.author: Pope John Paul II
items.summary: Written for the International Year of the Family, this letter is addressed to families themselves rather than to clergy. It presents the family as the school of the "civilization of love," marriage as a "sincere gift of self," parents as the first educators who also are educated by their children, and the fourth commandment as binding parents and children alike. It is more personal and accessible than most magisterial documents.
items.caveats: Philosophical in style; some passages assume familiarity with John Paul II's personalist vocabulary.
items.citation: John Paul II. (1994). Gratissimam sane [Letter to families]. Holy See.

items.title: Shepherding a Child's Heart
items.author: Tedd Tripp
items.summary: A widely used Reformed Protestant parenting book. Tripp argues that behaviour flows from the heart, so parents should aim beyond outward compliance to the child's motives and orientation toward God. It stresses rich communication (encouraging, instructing, entreating, praying) and different emphases for early childhood, middle childhood and the teen years. It endures as a popular framework for heart-focused Christian parenting.
items.caveats: Endorses spanking ("the rod") for young children. Meta-analyses link spanking to worse child outcomes, not better (Gershoff & Grogan-Kaylor, 2016), and the American Academy of Pediatrics (2018) advises against it; many Christian readers adopt the book's heart emphasis while setting aside its use of corporal punishment.
items.citation: Tripp, T. (1995). Shepherding a child's heart. Shepherd Press.

items.title: Amoris Laetitia (On Love in the Family)
items.author: Pope Francis
items.summary: This post-synodal exhortation is notably practical. Chapter 4 is an extended commentary on 1 Corinthians 13 as a guide to daily married love (patience, kindness, not keeping score, dialogue). Chapter 5 treats welcoming new life, and Chapter 7, "Towards a Better Education of Children," covers knowing where one's children are without controlling them, forming habits and the will, correction as encouragement, patient realism, sex education, and passing on the faith. These chapters endure as accessible counsel for families of any background.
items.caveats: Chapter 8, on pastoral care for divorced and civilly remarried Catholics, has been widely debated; the chapters on marriage and child-rearing are not contested in the same way.
items.citation: Francis. (2016). Amoris laetitia [Post-synodal apostolic exhortation on love in the family]. Holy See.

plans.intro: The Parent Curriculum runs beside the children's. It has four parts: a reading and practice plan for each stage of a child's life, a marriage track that runs through all of them, a family program on the model of the Olweus school program, and a short core shelf for the first year. The aim is children who are ambitious and humble, cooperative and loving, honest, self-controlled and glad, raised in a home where the parents' own marriage is tended as carefully as the children. Readings mix the research, the clinical guides and the classics; caveats in the booklist say where the evidence is thin.

core.label: The core shelf
core.note: Twelve readings for every parent, about one a month in the first year of the program, whatever the children's ages. Each stands for a body of research or a tradition that the stage plans build on.

stages.label: Before birth
stages.focus: The couple prepares for the largest change a marriage goes through. Relationship satisfaction falls on average after the first child; programs that prepare couples in pregnancy soften the fall and protect the baby from parental conflict and depression.
aims: Agree how the work of the household and the night will be shared
Learn to soothe each other and to repair after conflict before sleep is short
Know the signs of depression in either parent and where help is found
Plan the mother's nutrition and exercise (see the gestation plan)
practices: A weekly half-hour couple meeting (the marriage track) from the first trimester

practices.A written plan for the first six weeks a: night feeds, visitors, meals, who holds what

practices: The gestation plan's nutrition and exercise, week by week
stages.help: Low mood, anxiety or intrusive thoughts lasting more than two weeks in either parent, or any thought of self-harm, call for the obstetric provider or a clinician the same week.

stages.label: The first year
stages.focus: Sensitive, responsive care builds secure attachment, the base from which a child later explores, learns and trusts. Short, focused programs that raise parents' sensitivity work as well as long ones.
aims: Respond promptly and warmly to the baby's signals, and read them better each month
Keep the marriage close while sleep is short; share the night
Begin family prayer and simple rhythms of the day
practices: Daily floor time and talk with the baby, face to face, without screens
A short evening check-in between the parents on how each is coping
Family prayer at a fixed time each day
stages.help: Postpartum depression can begin any time in the first year, in mothers and in fathers; persistent exhaustion, hopelessness or withdrawal from the baby call for help, as does conflict that the couple can no longer repair on its own.

stages.label: Toddlers
stages.focus: The toddler begins to want to help and to say no. Warm, mutually responsive parenting at this age predicts later conscience and cooperation; rewards for helping can crowd out the child's own wish to help.
aims: Welcome the child's helping, without paying for it
Name feelings and set calm, consistent limits
Hold the line against harsh punishment and shouting
practices: Small real jobs every day (practical life at home)
The family meal, with the toddler at the table
One-to-one play time with each parent, child-led, a few minutes daily
stages.help: Tantrums that are daily, long and violent past age three, or a parent's sense of losing control, are well treated by parent-child interaction therapy or a similar evaluated program.

stages.label: Early childhood
stages.focus: Self-control, honesty and empathy grow fast. Children lie more in punitive homes and tell the truth more when honesty is praised; emotion coaching and authoritative discipline give the best long-run results.
aims: Coach emotions rather than dismiss them
Praise effort and honesty, not cleverness
Begin the family program's rules and weekly meeting
practices: The four family rules and a short weekly family meeting (the family program)
Daily read-aloud of fables and virtue stories
Family games that need turn-taking and good losing
stages.help: Persistent defiance, aggression or fears that disrupt daily life respond well to evaluated parent-training programs; the Family Check-Up is a light first step.

stages.label: Middle childhood
stages.focus: Competence, conscience and friendship. Autonomy-supportive parenting builds the child's own motivation; praise for intelligence weakens it, and inflated praise breeds narcissism. Siblings learn to quarrel well or badly, and kindness can be practised.
aims: Support autonomy within firm expectations
Praise process and effort, and keep praise honest
Teach siblings to solve problems together
Let children take real risks and real responsibility
practices: Children take a role in the weekly family meeting (chair, scribe, timekeeper) by age
Weekly acts of kindness, chosen by the children, reported at the meeting
Growing freedom outdoors and in town, step by step
stages.help: Bullying, persistent anxiety or school refusal, or a sibling who is repeatedly hurt, call for action and often for outside help.

stages.label: Adolescence
stages.focus: The adolescent brain is unusually open to learning and to risk. Teens who are known, trusted and given responsibility do best; family dinners, gratitude and limits on phones help, though the evidence on screens is debated.

aims.Stay close: shared meals, one-to-one time, interest in the teen's world

aims: Hand over responsibility on a plan, so the teen is ready to leave at 18
Keep phones and social media out of bedrooms and meals
practices: Family dinner most nights, phones away
A yearly conversation with each teen on the next year's freedoms and duties
Service and leadership outside the family (the children's service units)
stages.help: Depression, self-harm, substance use or a breakdown of trust need prompt professional help; evaluated family programs such as the Strengthening Families Program and the Family Check-Up also work at this age.

stages.label: Adult children and the next generation
stages.focus: The task turns to friendship with adult children, to a marriage alone again in the house, and to the role of grandparents, who help children's health and development when they are involved and supportive.
aims: Treat adult children as adults, with advice when asked
Renew the marriage for the years after the children leave
Be present as grandparents without displacing the parents
practices: A family gathering on the great feasts each year
The marriage track's yearly retreat continues
stages.help: Estrangement or long-running family conflict is a reason for family therapy rather than silence.

marriage.label: The marriage track
marriage.note: The parents' marriage is the child's first school of love and of conflict. Children are harmed less by disagreement than by hostile, unresolved conflict, and couples who learn a few skills early keep their friendship through the hardest years.
practices: Daily: a 20-minute conversation at the end of the day about stress outside the marriage, listening first (Gottman).
Weekly: a half-hour couple meeting: what went well, one issue handled with the speaker-listener technique (PREP), and the week ahead.
Monthly: an evening out alone together.
Yearly: a weekend retreat to review the marriage, the children and the coming year.
In conflict: soft start-ups, breaks before flooding, and repair before sleep.
marriage.help: Couples counseling works best early, before contempt sets in. Emotionally focused couples therapy and PREP-based programs have the strongest evidence; online programs such as OurRelationship help couples who cannot reach a therapist.

family.label: The family program
family.note: Modelled on the Olweus Bullying Prevention Program, which works at the levels of the whole school, the classroom and the individual child, and on the Good Behavior Game. The family version has the same three levels. Using school programs this way is an analogy, not a tested family intervention; each part draws on research cited in the booklist.

levels.label: The whole family
parts: Four family rules, adapted from the four Olweus rules: we do not hurt or belittle one another; we help anyone in the family who is being treated badly; we include anyone who is left out; we tell a parent when someone is being hurt.
Warm, consistent consequences: praise and attention for keeping the rules, small and immediate consequences for breaking them, never harsh or humiliating (Kazdin; AAP).
Family routines that hold the week together: daily meals, bedtime reading, the Sunday rhythm.
A short yearly family questionnaire, as in the Olweus program, so each child can say privately how home is going.

levels.label: The weekly family meeting
parts: Appreciations first: each member names something good another did.
The calendar and the week's jobs.
One problem, solved together: the children propose rules and consequences; the parents decide.
A family goal for the week, and the Good Behavior Game for children under ten: the family as one team earns a small shared privilege for a good week.
Roles rotate by age: the youngest leads appreciations, older children chair and keep notes.

levels.label: Each child
parts: One-to-one time with each parent every week.
A private talk when a rule is broken or a child is hurt, aimed at repair, not shame.
Responsibilities and freedoms that grow each year, agreed at a yearly review.

children.role: Learns the four rules, leads appreciations, has a daily job.
Keeps time or notes at the family meeting, proposes the week's kindness project, helps a younger sibling.
Chairs the family meeting in turn, mentors a younger sibling, leads one family service project a year.

pregnancy.title: Gestation and the first year: nutrition and exercise
pregnancy.scope: Preconception, the three trimesters, the postpartum months and the baby's first year of feeding. The "first 1,000 days" run from conception to the second birthday; this plan covers the first roughly 640 of them (the months before conception, about 280 days of pregnancy and 365 days of infancy). Feeding in the second year is outside this file.
pregnancy.disclaimer: General educational guidance for healthy adults with uncomplicated singleton pregnancies, drawn from the public guidelines listed under sources. It is not medical advice and does not replace care from an obstetrician, midwife, pediatrician or registered dietitian. Follow the obstetric and pediatric providers' instructions whenever they differ from this plan. Many conditions change the advice on food, supplements or exercise, including pre-eclampsia or gestational hypertension, gestational or pre-existing diabetes, placenta previa, cervical insufficiency or cerclage, preterm labor or ruptured membranes, unexplained bleeding, fetal growth restriction, twins or higher-order multiples, anemia, thyroid disease, heart or lung disease, an eating disorder, bariatric surgery, a prior neural-tube-defect pregnancy, anti-seizure or other folate-blocking medication, vegan diets, food allergy, and a cesarean or complicated birth. Before starting or changing an exercise program in pregnancy, a clinical evaluation by the obstetric provider is recommended (acog-804). In an emergency, call 911 or the local emergency number.

evidenceLevels.established: A recommendation published by ACOG, AAP, WHO, USPSTF, the National Academies (IOM), the US Dietary Guidelines, FDA/EPA, CDC, NIAID or the American Thyroid Association, current as of the lastReviewed date.
evidenceLevels.emerging: Supported by randomized trials, systematic reviews or expert consensus statements, but not part of a standard US guideline, or the trial evidence is mixed. Worth discussing with the provider; not a requirement.

brainDevelopment.summary: Calories are essential for growth but are not sufficient for normal brain development. The nutrients with the strongest effects on the developing brain are protein; zinc; iron; choline; folate; iodine; vitamins A, D, B6 and B12; and long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids such as DHA (aap-1000-days, georgieff-2007). Brain regions develop on different timetables: the neural tube closes within the first month after conception; myelination rises sharply from about 32 weeks of gestation and is most active in the first two years; the hippocampus (memory) begins its rapid growth phase at about 32 weeks and continues for at least 18 months after birth; the prefrontal cortex begins its growth spurt in the first six months after birth (cusick-georgieff-2016). Maternal stress and poor nutrition interact and each can worsen the other's effect on infant neurocognitive development (monk-2013).

windows.when: At least 1 month before conception through the first 2-3 months of pregnancy
windows.role: The neural tube (future brain and spinal cord) forms and closes about 26-28 days after fertilization, often before a pregnancy is recognized. Folic acid taken before and in early pregnancy prevents neural tube defects.

windows.when: Before conception and throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding; most critical in the first trimester
windows.role: Iodine's only role in brain development is making thyroid hormone. In the first trimester the fetal brain depends entirely on the mother's thyroxine (T4), so maternal iodine status at conception matters. Severe deficiency causes cretinism; milder deficiency is linked with lower cognitive scores.

windows.when: Throughout pregnancy and lactation; research interest concentrates on the third trimester
windows.role: Choline is needed for cell membranes, the neurotransmitter acetylcholine and methyl metabolism alongside folate. Animal studies show lifelong cognitive benefits in offspring when the maternal diet is supplemented with choline, and the AAP and AMA have emphasized prenatal choline. Human evidence is still small: a controlled-feeding trial of 26 women found faster infant information processing when mothers ate about 930 mg a day versus 480 mg a day in the third trimester.

windows.when: Throughout pregnancy, especially the third trimester, and from about 4-6 months of infancy
windows.role: Iron is required for normal fetal brain anatomy, myelination, the dopamine, serotonin and norepinephrine systems and hippocampal energy metabolism. Prevention is preferred to treatment, and the earlier the brain is protected (prenatal period and early infancy) the better; excess or mistimed iron can also harm.

windows.nutrient: DHA and other long-chain omega-3 fats
windows.when: Pregnancy (rapid brain growth from the third trimester) through breastfeeding and the first two years
windows.role: DHA is needed for neurogenesis, neuronal migration, membrane function and synapse formation. Seafood intake in pregnancy is associated with better cognitive measures in young children, but supplement trials of child cognition show mixed results in meta-analyses.
Fetal growth restriction and growth failure in the first years are consistently linked with poorer neurodevelopment; protein affects the hippocampus and cortex as well as global development.

windows.when: While trying to conceive and the whole of pregnancy
windows.role: There is no known safe amount or safe time to drink. Alcohol causes fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, with growth and central nervous system effects possible at any point in pregnancy.

weightGain.note: Totals assume about 1.1-4.4 lb (0.5-2 kg) gained in the first trimester; weekly rates apply to the second and third trimesters. Twin ranges are provisional.

dailyTargets.pregnancy: 600 mcg DFE (with a 400-800 mcg folic acid supplement)
220 mcg (ATA: about 250 mcg from all sources)
dailyTargets.lactation: 290 mcg (ATA: about 250 mcg from all sources)

dailyTargets.pregnancy: 71 g (1.1 g/kg) in the second half

stages.label: Before conception (3+ months)
stages.weeks: 3 or more months before trying to conceive
stages.focus: The neural tube closes 26-28 days after fertilization and the major organs form in the first 8 weeks, often before a pregnancy is known, so the most important nutrition happens before conception: folic acid every day, adequate iodine stores for the first-trimester thyroid supply to the fetal brain, a varied whole-food diet, no alcohol, and reaching a healthy weight and fitness base. A strong aerobic and strength base now makes it easier to keep exercising through pregnancy.
stages.energy: No extra calories. Aim to begin pregnancy at a healthy BMI (18.5-24.9); underweight raises the risk of low birth weight and preterm birth, and overweight or obesity raises the risks of pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, cesarean birth and neural tube defects. Even a small loss of excess weight before pregnancy improves health (acog-faq-prepregnancy, iom-2009-gwg).

nutrients.name: Folic acid
nutrients.amount: 400-800 mcg a day, starting at least 1 month (ideally 3) before conception
nutrients.why: Prevents neural tube defects. Nearly half of US pregnancies are unplanned, so the USPSTF advises it for everyone who could become pregnant. A prior NTD-affected pregnancy calls for 4 mg a day from 3 months before conception, as a separate prescription.
nutrients.foods: Fortified cereal, enriched bread and pasta, beans and lentils, dark leafy greens, oranges, peanuts

nutrients.name: Iodine
nutrients.amount: Supplement of 150 mcg a day (as potassium iodide), ideally from at least 3 months before conception
nutrients.why: Builds thyroid hormone supply for the first trimester, when the fetal brain depends on maternal T4. Many prenatal vitamins contain little or no iodine, so the label should be checked. Avoid supplements above 500 mcg a day.
nutrients.foods: Iodized salt (used in place of plain salt, not in addition), milk, yogurt, cheese, eggs, seafood

nutrients.name: Prenatal vitamin
nutrients.amount: One daily serving as labeled
nutrients.why: Covers folic acid, iron and most vitamins. Taking a vitamin before and during pregnancy also reduces the risk of severe nausea and vomiting. Never double the dose: excess vitamin A can cause birth defects.
nutrients.foods: Not a substitute for food; choose an established brand and check for folic acid and iodine

nutrients.name: Seafood (omega-3 fats)
nutrients.amount: 2-3 servings (8-12 oz) a week of low-mercury fish
nutrients.why: Builds omega-3 status before pregnancy; ACOG advises the same intake before, during and after pregnancy.
nutrients.foods: Salmon, sardines, trout, herring, anchovies, Atlantic mackerel, pollock, shrimp, canned light tuna

nutrients.name: Iron
nutrients.amount: 18 mg a day
nutrients.why: Enters pregnancy with iron stores; blood volume rises sharply later.
nutrients.foods: Lean red meat, poultry, fish, beans and lentils, iron-fortified cereals; eat with vitamin C foods

eat: Half of each plate vegetables and fruit; half of grains whole grain (acog-faq-nutrition)
Protein at every meal: eggs, fish, poultry, meat, beans, lentils, tofu, nuts and seeds (acog-faq-nutrition, dga-2025)
Dairy or a fortified alternative 2-3 times a day for calcium and iodine (acog-faq-nutrition, ods-iodine)
Two or three fish meals a week from the FDA Best Choices list (fda-fish)
Water as the main drink
limit: Alcohol: stop while trying to conceive; there is no known safe amount at any point in pregnancy (cdc-alcohol-pregnancy, dga-2025)
Tobacco, nicotine, marijuana and non-medical drug use: stop before pregnancy (acog-faq-prepregnancy)
Sugar-sweetened drinks and highly processed snacks: replace with whole foods (dga-2025, acog-faq-prepregnancy)
High-mercury fish: king mackerel, marlin, orange roughy, shark, swordfish, Gulf of Mexico tilefish, bigeye tuna (fda-fish)
Extra doses of vitamin A or multiple multivitamins (acog-faq-nutrition)

exercise.dose: 150-300 min a week moderate (brisk walking, cycling, swimming), or 75-150 min vigorous, or a mix
exercise.notes: Builds the cardiovascular base; any amount is better than none; replace sitting time with movement.

exercise.dose: 2 or more days a week, all major muscle groups
exercise.notes: Squats, hinges (deadlift pattern), rows, presses, carries; strengthening abdominal and back muscles helps prevent the low back pain common later in pregnancy.

exercise.dose: Learn correct technique now; daily practice
exercise.notes: Contract (squeeze and lift) and fully relax the pelvic floor; a pelvic health physiotherapist can confirm technique.

weeklyPlan.session: Strength 40 min (squat, hip hinge, row, push-up or press, carry; 2-3 sets of 8-12)
Brisk walk or run 30-40 min
Cycling or swimming 30-40 min, including some vigorous intervals if already fit
Strength 40 min (lunge, step-up, deadlift, pull-down or row, plank, side plank)
Brisk walk 30 min
Longer activity 45-60 min: hike, bike ride, sport
Rest or gentle stretching and yoga
Pelvic floor practice; break up long sitting

Bland, low-fat foods when nauseated (bananas, rice, applesauce, toast); whatever stays down is the right food (acog-faq-nvp)
8-12 cups of fluid a day, sipped through the day (acog-faq-nvp, acog-faq-nutrition)

stages.label: Second trimester
stages.focus: Steady fetal growth and placental expansion; maternal blood volume rises, so iron needs are high. Appetite usually returns, which makes this the trimester to build habits: protein, iron, choline, iodine and seafood every week. Exercise usually feels best now; the main adjustments are avoiding long periods flat on the back and anything with fall or impact risk.

nutrients.foods: Lean beef, turkey, shrimp, sardines, beans, lentils, fortified cereal; pair with vitamin C foods

nutrients.name: Choline

nutrients.why: Fetal brain and spinal cord development; most pregnant women in the US eat less than the Adequate Intake.
nutrients.foods: Eggs, beef, chicken, fish, milk, soybeans, peanuts

nutrients.name: Iodine
nutrients.amount: 220 mcg RDA; 150 mcg supplement
nutrients.why: Thyroid hormone for fetal brain development throughout pregnancy.
nutrients.foods: Dairy, eggs, seafood, iodized salt

nutrients.name: Calcium and vitamin D

nutrients.why: Fetal bones and teeth.

nutrients.foods: Eggs, dairy, fish, poultry, meat, beans, lentils, tofu, nuts

Two or three fish meals a week; one could be canned salmon or sardines on toast (fda-fish)
Eggs several times a week for choline (ods-choline)
Iron-rich protein most days, with a vitamin C fruit or vegetable at the same meal (acog-faq-nutrition)
Fiber, fluids and activity to ease constipation (acog-faq-exercise-pregnancy, acog-faq-nutrition)

Sugar-sweetened beverages and foods high in added sugar or saturated fat (dga-2025, acog-faq-nutrition)

exercise.notes: Walking, swimming, water aerobics, stationary cycling, dancing; experienced runners and racquet players may continue with the provider's agreement.

exercise.dose: Whole pregnancy

stages.label: Third trimester
stages.focus: The brain growth spurt begins: myelination rises sharply and the hippocampus enters its rapid growth phase from about 32 weeks, and the fetus builds the iron stores it will rely on in early infancy. Iron, choline, iodine, DHA and protein matter most now. Exercise continues with lower impact as balance and comfort change, with water exercise a good option for back pain.
stages.energy: About +452 kcal a day (dga-2020), for example adding both a mid-morning and an evening snack. Weekly gain as in the second trimester (iom-2009-gwg). Sessions longer than 45 minutes or at high intensity can lower blood sugar, so eat beforehand or shorten the session (acog-804).

nutrients.name: Iron
nutrients.amount: 27 mg a day; more only if the provider finds deficiency
nutrients.why: Iron supports fetal brain anatomy, myelination and neurotransmitter systems; late-pregnancy stores protect the infant until iron-rich foods begin.
nutrients.foods: Red meat, poultry, fish, beans, fortified cereals, with vitamin C foods

nutrients.name: Choline

nutrients.why: Fetal growth and the building of fetal bones and teeth.

stages.label: Postpartum and breastfeeding (the mother)
stages.weeks: Birth to 12 months after birth; recovery focus in weeks 0-12
stages.focus: Recovery, milk production and a gradual return to full fitness. Breast milk carries the mother's iodine, choline and DHA to the infant brain during its fastest growth, so lactation nutrition stays high-priority. Postpartum care is a process: contact with a maternal care provider within the first 3 weeks and a comprehensive visit no later than 12 weeks after birth (acog-736). Exercise resumes gradually, starting with pelvic floor work and walking, and building to at least 150 minutes a week plus strength training.
stages.energy: Breastfeeding: about +330 kcal a day in months 0-6 and +400 kcal a day in months 7-12 (dga-2020). Return toward pre-pregnancy weight gradually; very low energy intake can affect milk and recovery, and energy availability is one of the factors used to adjust a return-to-running plan (delphi-run-program-2024).

nutrients.name: Choline

stages.label: Baby, birth to 6 months
stages.focus: Breast milk alone for about the first 6 months, or iron-fortified infant formula when breast milk is not available. The infant brain is in its fastest growth: myelination is most active, the hippocampus is in its rapid growth phase and the prefrontal cortex begins its growth spurt in these months (cusick-georgieff-2016). Two supplements matter: vitamin D for all breastfed babies, and iron from about 4 months for exclusively breastfed babies.
stages.energy: Feed on demand; breast milk or formula is the complete diet. Growth is tracked by the pediatrician at well visits. No water, juice or solid foods are needed in the first 6 months for most infants (dga-2025, aap-breastfeeding-2022).

nutrients.name: Breast milk (or iron-fortified formula)
nutrients.amount: Exclusively for about 6 months
nutrients.why: The AAP recommends exclusive breastfeeding for about 6 months, then continued breastfeeding with complementary foods for as long as mutually desired, to 2 years or beyond.
nutrients.foods: Breast milk; iron-fortified infant formula when breast milk is unavailable

nutrients.name: Vitamin D
nutrients.amount: 400 IU a day by mouth, starting shortly after birth
nutrients.why: Breast milk usually does not supply enough vitamin D; also applies to infants drinking less than 32 oz of formula a day.
nutrients.foods: Infant vitamin D drops

nutrients.name: Iron

Daily vitamin D drops (aap-vitd-2008)

Fruit juice before 12 months (aap-juice-2017)
Cow's milk, plant milks, water and solid foods as routine feeds before about 6 months unless the pediatrician advises (dga-2025, dga-2020)
Added sugars (dga-2025)

exercise.notes: Stroller walks count; follow the postpartum returnToExercise phases.

stages.label: Baby, 6 to 12 months
stages.focus: Complementary foods begin at about 6 months, while breast milk or formula remains the main nutrition to 12 months. Iron- and zinc-rich foods come first because infant iron stores are low and the brain's demand is high. Common allergens are introduced with other foods at about 6 months. A wide variety of textures and flavors, offered repeatedly, builds acceptance (it can take 8-10 exposures).
stages.energy: Continue breastfeeding or formula on demand; solids start as small tastes and grow to regular meals. Watch the baby's hunger and fullness cues (dga-2025).

nutrients.name: Iron
nutrients.amount: 11 mg a day (RDA, 7-12 months)
nutrients.why: Most iron must now come from food; iron supports myelination and neurotransmitter systems.
nutrients.foods: Pureed or finely minced meat, poultry and fish; iron-fortified infant cereal; mashed beans and lentils

nutrients.name: Common allergens
nutrients.amount: Introduce at about 6 months (not before 4 months) and keep offering
nutrients.why: Early introduction of peanut and egg prevents allergy to them; delaying allergenic foods does not prevent allergy. Peanut, egg, nut butters, shellfish and wheat are introduced along with other foods.
nutrients.foods: Thinned smooth peanut butter, well-cooked egg, finely ground or thinned nut butters, wheat cereal, cooked fish and shellfish

nutrients.name: Fish and DHA
nutrients.amount: Regular small portions of low-mercury fish
nutrients.why: Seafood supplies DHA, iodine, protein and zinc; choose from the FDA Best Choices list.
nutrients.foods: Salmon, sardines, trout, cod, pollock, flaked and boneless

nutrients.name: Vitamin D
nutrients.amount: 400 IU a day
nutrients.why: Continue drops for breastfed infants and those on less than 32 oz of formula a day.
nutrients.foods: Drops; salmon, egg yolks

nutrients.name: Full-fat dairy
nutrients.amount: Yogurt and cheese as foods
nutrients.why: Energy and nutrients for growth and brain development; cow's milk as a drink waits until 12 months.
nutrients.foods: Plain full-fat yogurt, soft pasteurized cheese

eat: Signs of readiness: sits up alone or with support, controls head and neck, grasps and brings objects to the mouth, opens the mouth for food, moves food to the back of the tongue and swallows rather than pushing it out (dga-2025)
First foods: meat, poultry or fish purees, iron-fortified cereal, vegetables, fruits, legumes, full-fat yogurt (dga-2025, aap-iron-2010)
Progress from smooth to mashed, lumpy and soft finger foods (dga-2025)
Offer a new food many times; 8-10 tries may be needed (dga-2025)
Family foods without added salt or sugar, cut to safe sizes

exampleDay.breakfast: Breast milk or formula; iron-fortified oat cereal mixed with breast milk, mashed banana
exampleDay.lunch: Minced chicken with mashed sweet potato; soft-cooked green beans
exampleDay.snack2: Plain full-fat yogurt with thinned smooth peanut butter
exampleDay.dinner: Flaked salmon, mashed lentils, soft-cooked carrots; strips of well-cooked egg omelet
exampleDay.notes: An example for about 9-12 months; at 6 months, start with one or two small tastes a day. Breast milk or formula stays the main source of nutrition.

limit: Honey before 12 months (dga-2020)
Cow's milk as a drink before 12 months; stop infant formula at 12 months and switch to whole milk (dga-2025, dga-2020)
Fruit juice before 12 months (aap-juice-2017)
Added sugars and highly processed or nutrient-poor foods (dga-2025)
Choking hazards: whole nuts, whole grapes, popcorn, hot dog rounds, hard raw vegetables, globs of nut butter (dga-2020)
High-mercury fish (fda-fish)
Caffeinated drinks (dga-2025)

exercise.dose: At least 150 min moderate (or 75 min vigorous) aerobic activity a week plus 2+ strength days
exercise.notes: Running, sport and heavier lifting can resume progressively; volume before intensity; continue pelvic floor training.

exercise.dose: Every session
exercise.notes: Feed or express before exercise, hydrate, and adjust training for sleep, mood and energy availability.

warnings: Call 911 for signs of a severe allergic reaction after a new food: trouble breathing, widespread hives, facial swelling, repeated vomiting, limpness.
Always seat the baby upright and supervise eating; learn infant choking first aid.
Infants with severe eczema or a known food allergy need an allergen plan from the pediatrician or allergist (niaid-peanut-2017, allergy-consensus-2021).
